title: Invasive species' environmental impacts are more severe in the Global South.
data_url: https://zenodo.org/records/21509968 (GIDIAS v1.1, the underlying database); paper's own code+data bundle at https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.70rxwdcct

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Dryad listing via API: Code_Data_Bacher-etal2026.zip (15.9 MB) plus README, CC0. Both downloads refused to scripts (401 from the API, 403 from the file stream), so I read the README only through the landing page. Downloaded and parsed the GIDIAS (Global Impacts Dataset of Invasive Alien Species) v1.1 CSV from Zenodo (28.9 MB, CC-BY-4.0, dated 2026-07-23) and its metadata sheet. Counts: 22,865 rows × 94 columns, 0 duplicate IDs, 0 duplicate rows. 11,881 rows have magnitude.Nature (0–3): 2,163 / 3,920 / 4,541 / 1,257. Of those, 10,555 have a text excerpt and 11,860 a year (1882–2022; 2,020 from 2018 or later). They cover 1,434 species, 266 locations, 96 assessors and 4,206 references. 644 repeated reference×species×affected-species groups exist, and 126 of them disagree on magnitude. Share of excerpts mentioning extinct/decline/reduce words rises from 5% (level 0) to 39% (level 3).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The Science paper's country-level severity metric, its governance regressions and its country-aggregate tables (GIDIAS_20250417_agg_regions.csv and nine regression datasets) are known only from the Dryad README and abstract; not opened. Paper full text not available (no PMCID). Which GIDIAS snapshot (20250417) the paper used versus v1.1 is from the README.

a1_downloadable.note: GIDIAS v1.1 CSV downloaded directly from Zenodo without login. The paper's own Dryad zip is public CC0 but refused scripted download (401/403). Our project does not need it.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: magnitude.Nature is a column: the EICAT (IUCN Environmental Impact Classification for Alien Taxa) impact level, 0–3, filled for 11,881 rows. It needs no construction. Checked in the file.

a3_inputs_present.note: Text.excerpt (median 194 characters) is present for 10,555 labelled rows. Taxonomy, realm, impact mechanism, country, habitat flags and year are all in-table. Checked in the file.

a4_units_stated.note: Ordinal scale defined in the metadata sheet: 0 no impact, 1 individual performance down, 2 population down, 3 local/global extinction.

a5_enough_rows.note: 11,881 labelled impact records (10,555 with text). This is a 4-class ordinal classification. Counted in the file.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Whole table fits in memory easily; sentence embeddings of about 10.5k short excerpts run on CPU in minutes.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The GIDIAS paper says more than 22,000 records and 3,353 species. The v1.1 file has 22,865 rows and 3,386 GBIF-verified names (GBIF: Global Biodiversity Information Facility), a small v1.0→v1.1 update with a change log on Zenodo.

a8_label_provenance.note: The level was assigned by 96 human expert assessors reading the source literature, not by a model. The excerpt-to-level task mimics that human annotation (a legitimate automation target), so references must be held out to avoid shared-excerpt leakage.

B1.why: One 94-column CSV with a unique rowID; label, text and context in the same table (opened).

B2.why: pandas read the machine-readable CSV first try with utf-8 (verified).

B3.why: Single EICAT scale, but 96 assessors applied it; per-assessor bias likely and unmeasured.

B4.why: 10,984 rows lack magnitude and must be dropped; no censored values within the labelled rows.

B5.why: 644 repeated reference×species groups, 126 disagree; easy to group, not to resolve.

B6.why: Metadata sheet documents all 94 columns with format and unique-value counts (opened).

C1.why: Held-out-assessor and temporal transfer is informative either way; a plain accuracy number is less so.

C2.why: Two recent EICAT text classifiers exist, trained on GISD full texts, with no open GIDIAS-scale benchmark.

C3.why: Better/unique-application: 10k excerpt-level labels versus prior full-paper sets; angle moderate.

C4.why: EICAT assessment is manual expert reading of literature; the IPBES assessment needed 96 assessors.

C5.why: Majority-class and keyword baselines are trivial; Brinner & Zarrieß macro-F1 0.523 is on a different dataset.

D1.why: PubMedBERT / SciBERT / sentence-transformers text encoders are open and downloadable.

D2.why: Short excerpts; embed about 10.5k once on CPU, then fit a logistic or ordinal head.

D3.why: GIDIAS CC-BY-4.0 (Zenodo record); common biomedical text encoders under MIT/Apache licences.

E1.why: Group splits by reference (4,206), assessor (96) or species (1,434) are available in columns.

E2.why: 96 assessors and 283 species with ≥10 labelled rows give many holdout groups.

E3.why: Majority class (level 2, 38%) and per-mechanism mean computable from file.

E4.why: 126 of 644 repeated groups disagree (about 20%), which gives a rough agreement ceiling.

E5.why: Extinction-word frequency climbs 5%→39% across levels 0→3 (verified); the model must exceed it.

E6.why: Label shuffle and text-versus-metadata ablation are straightforward on one table.

E7.why: Year column (2,020 labelled rows from 2018 onward) allows a temporal split; IUCN GISD EICAT assessments are external.

E8.why: Prior classifiers used different datasets; the paper's country regressions are not ML numbers.

G1.why: GBIF-verified taxon names and country names/ISO3 codes, not numeric IDs; DOI present for only 3,723 labelled rows.

G2.why: World Bank governance indicators (WGI, Worldwide Governance Indicators) by country; GBIF occurrences; SInAS alien distributions by taxon name.

G3.why: Many records per country/species; collapse is by aggregation, with a manageable many-to-one join.

G4.why: Text plus governance tests whether severity differences survive excerpt content, adding moderately to the paper's question.

H1.why: Level 0 (no impact) has 2,163 rows and positive/neutral directions are recorded (verified).

H2.why: 266 locations, but USA alone is 4,870 of 22,865 rows; literature skewed to Global North.

H3.why: Claim is precise: reproduces expert EICAT coding of published excerpts, not field-truth impact.

H4.why: The Science paper's central point is the Global North reporting bias, so the gap is explicit.

I1.why: IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group, IPBES assessors, and UKCEH (Coole & August) building EICAT AI tools.

I2.why: A good triage model would speed up assessments, but assessors stay in the loop.

I3.why: Ordinal macro-F1 or weighted kappa roughly fits 'flag severe impacts for expert review'.

I4.why: Keyword rule carries real signal; ML likely helps somewhat beyond it, not dramatically.

J1.why: Frozen-encoder head, grouped and temporal splits, assessor-transfer evaluation: real modelling.

J2.why: Ecology/invasion biology outside core domain; excerpts are readable for sanity checks.

J3.why: Keyword baseline, then embeddings, then assessor-holdout analysis are each shareable.

J4.why: Plausibly two weeks but not formally stated.

J5.why: No kill date written in NOTES.md yet.

existing_models.name: Brinner & Zarrieß 2025, 'Efficient Scientific Full Text Classification: The Case of EICAT Impact Assessments' (arXiv 2502.06551): PubMedBERT/ModernBERT with evidence-sentence selection, plus Llama-3.1 8B
existing_models.score_and_split: Search summary reports PubMedBERT macro-F1 rising from 0.425 to 0.523 with an evidence selector, on full-text papers aligned to IUCN EICAT assessments. Split not retrieved.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract says using human evidence annotations, LLM-generated annotations or explainability scores to improve efficiency is still open.

existing_models.name: Coole & August (UKCEH) 2026, 'Accelerating EICAT Assessments Using AI' (Zenodo 22008438): prompted LLMs (GPT-OSS, Nova, Claude, Llama) via AWS Bedrock
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha and F1 against 22 annotators on GISD (Global Invasive Species Database) papers; exact numbers not retrieved.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract screening efficiency and cost-benefit still to be evaluated; portal not yet released.

backbone.name: PubMedBERT or all-MiniLM/SPECTER2 sentence encoders (frozen) + ordinal logistic head
backbone.licence: Data CC-BY-4.0; encoders MIT/Apache (check per model)

integration.partner_dataset: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators and GDP by country (the paper's own covariates); SInAS alien species distributions
integration.join_key: Country.Location → ISO3 country code; GBIF-verified taxon name
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the Global South severity gap persist after controlling for what the excerpt actually reports, or is part of it a difference in which impacts get written up and how assessors code them?

controls.positive_control: Extinction/decline keyword frequency rises 5%→39% from level 0 to 3 (verified); the model must beat this keyword baseline. Second control: predict Realm or IAS.Taxon from the excerpt, which should be easy.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle magnitude labels within the reference-grouped CV and confirm collapse to the 38% majority class; ablate text versus metadata-only features.
controls.external_validation: Temporal split (train before 2018, test 2018–2022: 2,020 rows), held-out assessors, and IUCN GISD species-level EICAT assessments.

honest_claim_h3: The model predicts the EICAT level that an IPBES expert assessor assigned to a published impact excerpt, not the true field severity, and only for impacts that were studied and written up, which skews toward the Global North.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short published description of an invasive species' effect to predict how severe experts rated that impact, from none to extinction.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is a roughly 200-character excerpt from a paper describing one invasive species' effect on native biodiversity, plus species group, habitat and country. 10,555 labelled excerpts (verified).
plain_idea.predict: The impact level 0–3 on the IUCN EICAT scale (no effect, individuals harmed, populations reduced, local extinction), as assigned by human expert assessors reading the source literature.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: IUCN and IPBES impact assessments are slow manual literature reads; a triage model could flag severe impacts first. Testing it on held-out assessors also measures how consistently experts apply the scale.

more_or_better_data.why: GIDIAS gives 10,555 excerpt-level labels across 1,434 species, versus prior work's full-paper sets aligned to GISD assessments (size not retrieved). Ours is likely larger but shorter-text.

confidence_score.why: 126 disagreeing duplicate groups and 96 assessors allow estimating label noise, but too few replicates for per-item calibration. Prior models' calibration was not checked.

models_beatable.why: Brinner & Zarrieß 2025 reached macro-F1 0.523 with PubMedBERT on a different dataset (split not retrieved); Coole & August 2026 use closed LLMs. Neither was evaluated on GIDIAS.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No existing model is runnable on the same data and split; the prior datasets are full papers and use different label units.

label_elsewhere.sources: IUCN GISD (Global Invasive Species Database) EICAT species assessments (known resource); Brinner & Zarrieß 2025 EICAT full-text dataset (found by search).
label_elsewhere.join_key: GBIF-verified species name; DOI for some references
label_elsewhere.why: Species-level EICAT assessments give an independent check of whether excerpt-level predictions aggregate to the official species category.

ambitious.why: Publishes tools that automate ecological evidence synthesis; it would need assessor-held-out kappa near the inter-assessor ceiling.

realistic.why: An open-access invasion-biology journal that publishes EICAT methodology and tooling; a benchmark plus assessor-consistency analysis fits.

fallback.journal: Ecological Informatics (or arXiv preprint + an NLP-for-science workshop)
fallback.why: Accepts partial or negative text-mining results, such as 'the keyword baseline is as good as embeddings'.

pitch.headline: 10,555 expert-coded invasive-impact excerpts in one 29 MB CC-BY table, with the severity label, year and assessor in columns.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: 96 named assessors, 1,434 species, 266 locations, 2,163 explicit 'no impact' records, and 126 measurable assessor disagreements, all verified in the Zenodo CSV.
pitch.the_win: Weighted kappa on held-out assessors close to the duplicate-agreement ceiling (about 80% agreement), clearly above the keyword baseline.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn how consistent EICAT coding is across assessors and eras, which bears directly on the Science paper's country-severity comparisons.
pitch.who_wants_it: IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group and the UKCEH EICAT-AI team (Coole & August), when deciding whether automated triage is trustworthy.

ml_idea: Embed GIDIAS text excerpts with a frozen biomedical sentence encoder, add taxonomy/realm/mechanism metadata, and fit an ordinal head for EICAT level 0–3. Evaluate with reference-grouped CV, a held-out-assessor split and a temporal split (before 2018 versus 2018 onward), against majority-class and keyword baselines. As a secondary analysis, test whether residual severity differs by Global South status.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: about 10.5k excerpts of about 200 characters at roughly 20/s for a BERT-base encoder on CPU gives about 10 minutes; logistic heads on 768-dimensional embeddings train in seconds per fold.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Run a TF-IDF + logistic baseline with reference-grouped and assessor-held-out CV. If held-out-assessor macro-F1 is near the 38% majority-class level, excerpts don't carry the label and the project dies.

verdict_reason: Clean, open, 11,881-row labelled table with text and assessor columns passes Part A on the files. Two recent EICAT text classifiers exist, though, and it's unverified whether short excerpts carry enough signal across assessors; run the grouped TF-IDF check first.
